Contributing to LDNDRC

Thanks for wanting to help. This project is a workshop platform built by people who had to run it in front of a room, so the bar is simple: if you claim it works, show the command that proves it.

You do not need to be a Kubernetes expert to contribute. Documentation, tests, and honest failure reports are as valuable as features.

The three laws

These are not style preferences. Every merge should respect them.

  1. The LAN comes first. Nothing may require the public internet to run a class. No cloud identity, no hosted database, no external registry at demo time.
  2. Isolation is a structural property. One student per pod, one namespace per session, DDS never crossing the pod boundary. Do not "fix" isolation with a firewall rule or a shared workspace.
  3. Least privilege, proven by command. The panel runs with namespace-scoped RBAC. A new permission needs a kubectl auth can-i line showing exactly what it grants.

Never contributed before? Take any row in docs/roadmap.md and shrink it until it is one afternoon of work. That is how this repo was built: 43 checkpoints, each one the smallest provable step.

Setup

Prerequisites: Go ≥ 1.26, Node ≥ 22 (docs site ≥ 20), Docker, kubectl, k3d.

bash
# optional, matches the repo's tool pins
mise install

# container access without sudo
sudo usermod -aG docker "$USER"
newgrp docker
docker ps

The fastest full-stack loop is the one-laptop demo in README.md (Path A) or docs/local-cluster-headlamp.md. You do not need a GPU or a second laptop for it.

The development loop

Control panel

bash
cd control-panel
go build ./...
go test ./...          # ~12s; internal/join covers the driver

Run it locally, outside any cluster, for API work. The three databases default to /var/lib/ldndrc/, which needs root on most machines — point them somewhere writable:

bash
mkdir -p /tmp/ldndrc-dev
JWT_SECRET=dev-only \
  CONTROL_PANEL_PORT=8087 \
  ADVERTISE_MDNS=false \
  SESSIONS_DB=/tmp/ldndrc-dev/sessions.json \
  NODES_DB=/tmp/ldndrc-dev/nodes.json \
  DOWNLOADS_DB=/tmp/ldndrc-dev/downloads.json \
  go run ./cmd/server

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8087/healthz    # {"status":"ok"}

Without in-cluster config the panel still serves login, sessions (recorded, not provisioned), node registration, the portal, and the gateway routes — enough to test auth, CSRF, validation, and handler behaviour. Anything that needs a real pod requires Path A.

The student UI must be built before go build embeds a real SPA. control-panel/web/dist/ is gitignored:

bash
cd control-panel/web
npm ci
npm run build

Images

bash
docker build -t ldndrc/control-panel:dev ./control-panel
docker build -t ldndrc/demo-standin:dev ./images/demo-standin
k3d image import ldndrc/control-panel:dev ldndrc/demo-standin:dev -c ldndrc

The workspace image is ~10 GB and takes a long time. Do not rebuild it to test a frontend change. Use demo-standin unless the change is actually inside the session.

Docs site

bash
cd docs-site
npm install
npm run build      # validates the graph, then writes dist/
npm run serve      # http://127.0.0.1:8090

Verification matrix

Pick the row that matches your change. Paste the command and its output in the PR.

Change Prove it with
Go logic cd control-panel && go test ./...
Panel boots JWT_SECRET=x go run ./cmd/server then /healthz
Manifest / RBAC kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f manifests/ + kubectl -n ldndrc auth can-i …
Session lifecycle Create a session, wait for ready, curl the editor host with and without the cookie (200 / 401)
Join detection ./test-join.sh and ./test-joining.sh
Captive redirect ./test-captive-trap.sh
Student UI cd control-panel/web && npm run build (runs tsc)
Docs site cd docs-site && npm run build (fails on a broken graph)
Anything user-visible A screenshot or a two-line before/after, not a description

If a check needs hardware you do not have, say so explicitly. "Not tested on a second laptop" is an acceptable sentence. "Should work" is not a verification.

Making a change

  1. Open an issue or leave a note first for anything bigger than a docs fix, so the design conversation does not happen inside a diff.

  2. Branch by intent: feat/<scope>, fix/<scope>, docs/<scope>.

  3. Keep the change one idea. A refactor mixed with a behavior change cannot be reviewed or reverted cleanly.

  4. Update the docs in the same commit. A feature with no operator instructions is not finished; this repo has been burned by that.

  5. Record the proof. For a milestone, add the next local_dev_docs/checkpoint-NN-<slug>.md using the existing checkpoints as the template: big picture, what got built, what was verified, what was not.

  6. Commit style (conventional-ish, lowercase scope):

    text
    feat(portal): register the onboarding page before approval
fix(csrf): exempt login from the CSRF guard
docs: checkpoint 43 records the captive harness promotion

  7. PR description: what changed, why, the verification output, and the known gaps. Link the roadmap row or checkpoint it closes.

Conventions

Go

  • Standard library first: net/http, client-go, encoding/json. Justify any new dependency in the PR.
  • Keep the package boundaries: internal/auth, sessions, nodes, gateway, portal, discovery, join. A handler that talks to Kubernetes directly is a smell — put it in internal/sessions.
  • Errors at the gateway have one meaning each: 401 no cookie, 404 no session, 503 provisioning, 502 unhealthy pod. Do not collapse them.
  • Tests are table-driven and hermetic. Do not require a live cluster for go test.

Kubernetes

  • One concern per manifest, and the filename says which concern.
  • RBAC stays namespace-scoped. Cluster-wide verbs need a written reason.
  • Session pods request nvidia.com/gpu only when the deployment says so; the demo path (SESSION_GPU_LIMIT=0) must keep working.
  • Never commit a Secret. secret.example.yaml documents the shape; the real value is created at deploy time.

UI

Five rules are in docs/uiux-design.md; the important ones for review: one primary action per screen, status is ambient (top bar), and the desktop is an escape hatch, not a default. Match the existing dark/warm visual language instead of introducing a second design system.

Docs and lessons

There are three shelves. Put the document on the right one.

Shelf Purpose Tone
docs/ Design and operations references Precise, current, command-first
local_dev_docs/ Historical checkpoints and the cheatsheet Past tense, receipts, honest gaps
docs-site/content/topics/ Taught lessons distilled from the two above One concept, prerequisites, a Verify command

Lesson voice: start with the problem, name the mechanism, state the failure mode, end with something the reader can run. A lesson that only links to another document is a stub and should not be marked shipped.

To add a topic:

  1. Add the node to docs-site/content/graph.json with domain, title, summary, status, minutes, requires, sources, glyph, and verify.
  2. Write docs-site/content/topics/<id>.md. Use [[other-topic-id]] for links.
  3. npm run build — it refuses unknown prerequisites, missing files, and cycles.
  4. Check the rendered route with Route to here.

Status is a claim: shipped = proven on real machines, partial = works in pieces with the gap named, designed = written down but not built. When in doubt, downgrade.

What will not be merged

  • A cloud dependency in the live path, or anything that breaks with the uplink down.
  • A second shared workspace, or an isolation change that relies on cooperation.
  • Secrets, private IPs, tokens, or machine-specific paths committed to the repo.
  • AUTO_APPROVE=true as a default, or any path that removes the human approval step.
  • "Done" without a command, a checkpoint, or a live proof.
  • Assets or CSS copied from vimjoyer.com/nixmap; the docs site re-implements the design from tokens.
  • A large speculative feature that is not on the roadmap and has no smallest slice.

Review checklist

For the author, before asking for review:

  • The change is one idea and its diff is readable.
  • go test ./... (and npm run build where relevant) passes.
  • The verification command is in the PR and its output is pasted.
  • Docs and the roadmap row are updated in the same commit.
  • Known gaps are stated, not hidden.
  • No secret, private address, or vendor-specific hack without a comment.

For the reviewer:

  • Does it keep the LAN-first and isolation laws?
  • Is the new permission or dependency justified?
  • Does the failure mode have a diagnosable status or log line?
  • Does the claim match the proof?

Where to start right now

From docs/roadmap.md, in order of impact:

  1. R2-final — durable panel state across a redeploy (PVC + safe rollout).
  2. R4 — the pretty 3D viewer instead of the raw data frame.
  3. R5 — a full two-laptop install rehearsal, end to end.
  4. R7 — encryption at rest, resource limits, operator dashboards.
  5. Docs — every designed topic on the map is an invitation to build or to sharpen the specification.

Getting unstuck

  • local_dev_docs/cheatsheet.md — "if X, run Y" for operators.
  • docs/project-journey-report.md — the plain-English architecture and glossary.
  • docs/roadmap.md — what is done, what is left, and why in that order.
  • The docs site (docs-site/) — the same material as a guided map, with a verify command on every topic.

Open an issue with the failing command, the output, and what you expected. A good bug report is a contribution in itself.
